title: Variational Quantum Conditional Boltzmann Machines for Time-Series Forecasting: Architectures, Symmetric Hyperparameter Evaluation, and a Nonlinear Benchmark
authors: Gerhard Hellstern, Danyal Maheshwari, Martin Zaefferer, Martin Braun, Tanja Döhler
abstract: In this study, we developed and evaluated four conditional energy-based forecasting architectures: a classical Gaussian-Bernoulli CRBM, a hybrid quantum-classical QCRBM, a full-register QQRBM, and a lag-feature QFeatureQRBM with complete derivations of their conditional distributions, Contrastive-Divergence gradients, and hybrid training, bridging the energy-based formulation and the implementation-level quantum computation. Unlike prior comparisons, our evaluation enforces symmetric hyperparameter optimisation: classical and quantum-specific hyperparameters receive an equally thorough grid search across thirteen structured experiments. We test on two data classes, a Gaussian-process dataset (GP) generated with real financial data and the input-driven NARMA-10 nonlinear benchmark. Across both regimes we find no systematic evidence of a quantum advantage at the available sample size: no quantum architecture improves on the best classical baseline. The fully quantum QQRBM and QFeatureQRBM are significantly worse, whereas the hybrid QCRBM is statistically indistinguishable from the strongest classical CRBM on both datasets. A power analysis bounds this null result: at n = 12 only medium-to-large effects are detectable, so small advantages cannot be excluded. An iso-parameter (matched-budget) comparison reaches the same conclusion: the classical CRBM is lowest at three of the four budgets and no CRBM-vs-QCRBM difference is significant at any budget.
summary: This paper rigorously compares Variational Quantum Conditional Boltzmann Machines against classical counterparts for time-series forecasting. Using extensive symmetric hyperparameter optimization across two datasets, the authors conclude that no definitive quantum advantage exists at current sample sizes. The best performance was consistently achieved by the strongest classical baseline model.
main_problem: The study compares classical energy-based models with quantum enhancements for time-series forecasting, aiming to find evidence of a quantum advantage.
main_result: No systematic evidence of a quantum advantage was found; the hybrid quantum architecture performed statistically indistinguishably from the best classical baseline across multiple rigorous tests.
method: The authors developed and evaluated four Variational Quantum Conditional Boltzmann Machine architectures using symmetric hyperparameter optimization on two distinct data benchmarks (GP and NARMA-10).
model_or_system: The core models are VQCBMs, including classical CRBM, hybrid QCRBM, full-register QQRBM, and lag-feature QFeatureQRBM. These build upon energy-based modeling principles for time-series prediction.
key_observables: Predictive accuracy measured by Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE) and $R^2$ across various budget constraints.
important_parameters: Sample size ($n=12$), hyperparameter budgets ($P \in\{84, 120, 156, 192\}$), and circuit depth/layers ($L_Q$).
main_assumptions: The comparison is limited by the available sample size, and the quantum path optimization was performed on a soft surrogate reconstruction loss rather than directly on the forecast objective.
figures_summary: Not specified in detail, but comparisons are made across various model classes (e.g., CRBM vs QCRBM) using NRMSE/R^2 tables for NARMA-10 and GP datasets.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the VQCBM architectures, details the derivations of conditional distributions and gradients, performs comprehensive symmetric hyperparameter optimization across 13 experiments on two data regimes, and concludes with performance comparisons under matched-budget analysis.
why_interesting: While focused on ML, the rigorous comparison between classical and quantum computational resources for complex time-series modeling touches upon the fundamental limits of computation in physical systems, which is relevant to understanding resource scaling in quantum simulation.
